6.0.0.en: 1 There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is common among men: 2 A man to whom God hath given riches, wealth, and honour, so that he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but a stranger eateth it: this is vanity, and it is an evil disease.

6.0.1.en: The wise man shows here how much evil befalls a man if he misuses God's gifts of money and wealth. He begins his discourse by saying: "There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is common among men" [1]. Perhaps Solomon, as a famous king to whom many came to hear his wisdom, saw an evil spreading among his people and among the strangers coming from the ends of the world; he saw it as a disease or plague that had settled in the hearts of many, the sickness of stinginess, which he calls "an evil disease" [2].

6.0.2.en: He saw a man "to whom God hath given riches, wealth, and honour, so that he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but a stranger eateth it" [1-2].

6.0.3.en: First: The writer affirms that the money and honor in this rich man's hands is God's gift, whether the man received it by the inheritance of his parents or gained it by his striving and toil... and it behooved him to thank God and praise Him, asking of Him wisdom and divine counsel that he might order his life well.

6.0.4.en: Second: This rich man has no excuse, for divine providence lavished blessings on him and he no longer lacked anything his heart desired, and as the Psalmist says: "Thou fillest their belly with thy hid treasure... As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness" (Ps 17:14-15). God in His love often gives the wicked the desire of their heart: temporal goods, and draws the heart of the believer to Himself to bear His likeness and image!

6.0.5.en: Third: This rich man did not enjoy what he received, leaving what he had to a stranger; perhaps he means that some stranger seizes his possessions, from which he deprives himself and his children of enjoyment, or that he dies without enjoying his wealth and has no son (or daughter) to inherit it, but a stranger takes possession of what he gathered... all that he gathered a stranger enjoyed!

6.0.6.en: Ephraim mixed with the pagan peoples and his life was corrupted, so it was said: "Strangers have devoured his wealth" (Hos 7:9), and the wise man speaks to the man who falls with a foreign (pagan) woman whose lips drop honey: "[Lest] thy labours be in the house of a stranger" (Prov 5:10). So sin in all its forms, especially greed and adultery, or the love of money and bodily pleasures, drives man into captivity, and the enemy of good robs him of all the divine gifts he carries; he loses his wealth, even his humanity, and is stripped of all reason and wisdom!

6.0.7.en: Sin is exceedingly sinful: its mouth drips honey and its words are smoother than oil, but like a two-edged sword it cuts into the depths to rob man even of himself! And the enemy of good takes possession of all his wealth!

6.1.s.en: 2. Wealth spoiled by the sense of want:

6.1.0.en: 3 If a man beget an hundred children, and live many years, so that the days of his years be many, and his soul be not filled with good, and also that he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he. 4 For he cometh in with vanity, and departeth in darkness, and his name shall be covered with darkness. 5 Moreover he hath not seen the sun, nor known any thing: this hath more rest than the other. 6 Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?

6.1.1.en: He gives another example, opposite to the first: a man who begets a hundred, or as the Psalmist says of some of the wicked, "They are full of children" (Ps 17:14), and lives a long time, and because of his greed feels want and dissatisfaction, since his soul remains in a state of emptiness; even if he thinks that he will have "no burial" [3], that is, that he will never die, the untimely birth is better than he, for he will not enjoy the sweetness of life but lives as in darkness because of his intense sense of need to hoard. He is like a tree that bears very many fruits, but does not offer its fruit to be eaten and keeps it on itself until it spoils and falls to the ground and gathers insects.

6.1.2.en: Perhaps he meant by "and also that he have no burial" that at his death he is "buried with the burial of an ass" (Jer 22:19); for although he has a hundred sons and lived many years gathering money, his children, because he deprived them of enjoying the goods all this time, do not care for his honor, nor do they concern themselves with his burial, but with searching for the wealth he left them and dividing it... I remember a family whose members quarreled over the inheritance among themselves while the body was still lying in a closed room, not yet buried! They were fighting instead of weeping for their father!

6.1.3.en: The wise man says of him: "An untimely birth is better than he" [3]. He concedes that the state of the untimely birth is extremely sad, "for he cometh in with vanity" [4], for in vain did the couple rejoice at the conception and the mother endure much awaiting her newborn, and the father prepared himself in mind and means for a happy event... and their hopes were disappointed, their spirits were broken and their efforts were lost in vain. "And departeth in darkness," for scarcely anyone is aware of him; before his birth could be celebrated he is buried without honor! "And his name shall be covered with darkness": the parents had prepared a name for him, which is not realized but vanishes with him into the darkness before anyone calls him by it: "Moreover he hath not seen the sun, nor known any thing" [5], that is, he did not look on the sun and enjoy the light, but went out from the darkness of the womb to the darkness of the grave, and no one knew of him, nor did he himself even recognize his parents.

6.2.0.en: This is the picture the wise man presented of the untimely birth, and yet in comparing him with the stingy man he says: "This hath more rest than the other. Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?" [5-6]. The untimely birth, deprived of the light of life and of every memory and of all knowledge... who has no social existence, is better than a stingy man who lives thousands of years hoarding money and sees no good in his life, and also awakens no happiness or joy in the lives of others... for after the misery of all these years he meets the untimely birth in the same place, "the grave"! The stingy man by his evil will has become like the untimely birth, coming in with vanity and going into darkness... for in vain does anyone hope for good from him; the love of money deprives him of seeing the Sun of righteousness and robs him of the ability to reason and of true spiritual knowledge! How dangerous is the love of money, for it makes man's life a hell and a darkness more bitter than the darkness of the grave... and finally he leaves the world naked, receiving nothing of all that he gathered.

6.2.1.en: * A camel cannot pass through the eye of a needle, nor the rich man enter the exalted Kingdom...

6.2.2.en: * Riches and gold do not remain with the one who acquires them; why does man acquire riches and gold that are not his?!

6.2.3.en: * Look at the rich who acquired names and greatness on earth: they have fallen, and their schemes and their names have come to nothing.

6.2.4.en: * The soul is greater than possessions and places.

6.2.5.en: * O my Lord, You are the wealth, the treasury and the treasure of him who possesses You; blessed is he who possesses nothing but You!

6.3.0.en: 7 All the labour of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled. 8 For what hath the wise more than the fool? what hath the poor, that knoweth to walk before the living? 9 Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire: this is also vanity and vexation of spirit. 10 That which hath been is named already, and it is known that it is man: neither may he contend with him that is mightier than he. 11 Seeing there be many things that increase vanity, what is man the better? 12 For who knoweth what is good for man in this life, all the days of his vain life which he spendeth as a shadow? for who can tell a man what shall be after him under the sun?

6.3.1.en: After the wise man revealed the danger of greed and the love of money, he goes on, as is his custom, to affirm that the money God gave us is given that we may use it, not that it may use us and enslave us.

6.3.2.en: "All the labour of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled" [7]. The money or wealth God gave us is given that we may eat and satisfy the needs of our body, but our souls are filled neither by food nor by the love of possessions, but by God Himself! The stingy man may deprive his mouth of food in order to gather money, and so neither his body nor his soul profits by it. Perhaps he means that however much the rich man gathers, he needs only to meet the needs of his body, with no difference between cheap food and luxurious... Then let him fill his mouth and the mouths of his brethren with the wealth he has!

6.3.3.en: Let the rich man fill his mouth with food and let him know that his soul will never be satisfied however much it hoards, because he that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver (Eccl 5:10)... his mouth needs food and his soul needs the love of God and of his neighbor.

6.3.4.en: Perhaps by his saying "All the labour of man is for his mouth" [7] he means that what the rich man gathers is only for the purpose of stopping his inner mouth that says, "Give, give"... but his mouth remains empty and his soul is not filled!

6.3.5.en: Finally, why does the rich man toil in vain, gathering money without satisfying his soul?! For the wise man is equal to the fool in leaving behind all that they own here, and so also the rich with the poor... only one thing remains, man's true wisdom in walking among the living (the sons of men) in a spirit of pure love.

6.3.6.en: "For what hath the wise more than the fool?

6.3.7.en: what hath the poor, that knoweth to walk before the living?"

6.3.8.en: The wise poor man lives happy, content with the food and clothing he has (1 Tim 6:8), and carries love with him into his eternity, while he who thinks himself wise and rich loses his happiness here and his eternal glory.

6.3.9.en: The Preacher's counsel to all is to walk in a spirit of thanksgiving, counting what they have, little or much, as better than waiting in a spirit of greed for what they desire and dream of in wealth and rank:

6.4.0.en: "Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire" [9]. The man who feels satisfied, content with what he has or with what is present before him, what he sees with his eyes, is better than he whose soul roams in covetousness, desiring things he may not be able to obtain.

6.4.1.en: * Be sure that the most foolish of all is he who finds satisfaction in no desire (asking for more); but the wise man is not found a captive to those desires.

6.4.2.en: St. Gregory the Wonder-worker Man's giving free rein to his desires, including the desire to possess, is "also vanity and vexation of spirit (a distress of the wind)" [9], because whenever he obtains something the flame of desire increases all the more to ask for more, and so he enters into distress of spirit! Therefore it behooves the believer to realize that what is in his hands has already been ordered for him by God, as his heavenly Father who loves him, and that He is almighty and all-wise... He knows how to give him what suits him. And if he wished to contend with Him, could he do so, when He is stronger than he and wiser and more loving? Can he change the plan of God his Father concerning him and alter His judgments?!

6.5.0.en: The Preacher says: "That which hath been is named already" [10], that is, that the Eternal, who was, had already called him by name as man. Man is unable to resist his mighty Creator... "Neither may he contend with him that is mightier than he" [10], that is, man cannot resist a stronger man, so can he resist the Creator of mankind?!

6.6.0.en: The Preacher closes his discourse with the final conclusion that what man gathers will not increase his happiness, because he does not know what is good for him [12], especially since his life, which he spends on earth, however long it is, is like a shadow [12], and he does not know what will happen after his death with regard to his family and offspring [12].

7.0.s.en: 1. A good name is better than luxury:

7.0.0.en: "A good name is better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one's birth" [1].

7.0.1.en: To acquire a name, a good reputation or a good fame is better than to acquire great wealth or costly perfume. The foolish man either hoards and gathers, so that neither he nor his sons nor his relative profit by what he has, or he squanders his money in extravagant living, living a life of pleasure and recklessness. But the wise man, in moderation, knows how to use the vain world without being enslaved by the world. He uses it without giving himself free rein in the love of money or the love of pleasures; he cares about the day of his death, to leave a true witness on earth, whose fragrance is better and more lasting than much costly perfume.

7.0.2.en: If the ointment here points to temporal goods, then a good name does not mean the love of passion or the seeking of vainglory, but leaving a living witness of a godly life, as happened with the woman who poured the ointment on the head of the Lord Christ, for He said: "Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, there shall also this, that this woman hath done, be told for a memorial of her" (Mt 26:13). This is the good name we acquire when we pour out our lives, poured forth like a flask of very costly ointment.

7.0.3.en: The wise man cares about the day of death, not the day of birth, and is not occupied with his temporal affairs like one who will remain in the world forever, but lifts his mind to what is beyond death, offering his life as a poured-out flask of ointment, whose fragrance spreads on earth and in heaven.

7.0.4.en: Our thinking about the day of birth is a regression to immature childhood, and a living in the dreams of the past, while our thinking about the day of death is an advance toward a deeper fellowship with the Lord Christ, who kindles our depths toward heavenly things, so that we bear death with Him every day with joy (1 Cor 15:13).

7.0.5.en: The natural man rejoices in the day of his birth and celebrates it as an annual feast, and fears the coming of the day of his death and makes every effort to postpone it as long as he can, but the spiritual man sees in the day of his birth a divine gift, and thanks the Creator who brought him into the world that He may bring him through the day of his death to a new birth, in which he meets Him face to face. The day of our birth brought us into the sufferings which we accept with thanksgiving for the sake of the Lord, but the day of death brings us into the perfect freedom of the glory of the children of God.

7.1.0.en: 2 It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart. 3 Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better. 4 The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth. 5 It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise, than for a man to hear the song of fools. 6 For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool: this also is vanity. 7 Surely oppression maketh a wise man mad; and a gift destroyeth the heart.

7.1.1.en: "It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart" [2].

7.1.2.en: In more than one place the Preacher urges us to rejoice and to remove grief from the heart (Eccl 11:9-10), for God establishes His Kingdom, the Kingdom of joy, within us. Here he speaks of repentance and preparation for eternity. In the house of mourning we see the end of the world as we see the open heaven, and long to pass over. The aim of funeral prayers is to comfort the loved ones of the departed and to open the doors of heaven before their hearts so that their souls may rejoice. The sorrow of repentance, which gives rise to inner peace, is better than the laughter of the reckless, and the sadness of countenance in the closet, not in our meeting with others, where remorse for sins gladdens the heart and makes it better!

7.1.3.en: Our awareness of the reality of death as an inevitable matter gives us a true, realistic appreciation of our temporal life and opens before us the door of hope in heavenly things, and also supports us in our spiritual striving... where we realize the shortness of the time of our sojourn, and our obligation to walk wisely and soberly instead of in excessive luxury and folly.

7.1.4.en: * An elder said: He is a fool who has in his mind the remembrance of anything of the world except the inheritance he alone will receive, I mean the grave.

7.1.5.en: St. John Saba * "It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting" [2].

7.1.6.en: In the first (house) we reap the merits of good work, and in the second, a fall into sin.

7.1.7.en: In one we hope for (eternal) recompense. In the second we actually receive the reward (luxury).

7.1.8.en: Sympathize with the sorrowing as though you too were sorrowful with them!

7.1.9.en: * If anyone wishes to rise, he must not seek the delights of the world, or pleasures, or luxuries, but everything that is full of pain and sorrow, for it is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting.

7.1.10.en: Truly Adam would not have descended from Paradise to the depths had he not been deceived by pleasure!

7.1.11.en: St. Ambrose * By the latter (going to the house of feasting) the soul is inflamed. For if we can keep pace with a life of luxury we slip into indulgence in pleasure, and if we cannot, we grieve. But in the house of mourning it is the opposite; if we cannot be luxurious we do not suffer for it, and if we can, we hold back from a life of luxury.

7.1.12.en: Monasteries are truly houses of mourning, where there are sackcloth and ashes; there is solitude, not laughter nor the pressures of temporal cares. There is fasting and sleeping on the ground; there is no rich, foul-smelling food there, no shedding of blood, nor agitation, nor disturbance, nor crowding.

7.1.13.en: St. John Chrysostom * Fix the matter of your departure in your heart, O man, by continually saying: "Behold, the messenger is coming to the doors, he who comes for me; why then am I slothful? My departure will be forever, and without return!

7.1.14.en: Spend the night in this thought, and let it gladden you all day long, so that when the time of departure draws near you receive it with welcome and joy, saying: [Come in peace, for I knew that you were coming, and I have not neglected anything that profits me on this road].

7.1.15.en: * The body cannot be persuaded to live long in a state of solitude as long as it is surrounded by the causes of worldly pleasures and ease. Nor can the mind cease from them (pleasures and ease) until the body is estranged from everything done in ease. For when the body beholds scenes of luxury and temporal things, and when every hour it sees causes of relaxation, an unruly desire for them is kindled in it.

7.2.0.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian "Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better" [3].

7.2.1.en: It behooves us, while we are still in this world and feel our weakness, to practice the sorrow of repentance daily, not the laughter of the reckless and the foolish, for the tears of repentance make our hearts better.

7.2.2.en: It is not to be understood from this that the believer lives wretched and gloomy-faced before others, but that he practices his repentance in his closet, in his private life, without crushing others with his grief!

7.2.3.en: The spiritual man grieves over his sin and does not lose his peace, and so he wins others by his cheerfulness springing from inner joy together with earnestness.

7.2.4.en: "It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise, than for a man to hear the song of fools.

7.2.5.en: For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool.

7.3.1.en: The man who is earnest in his life rejoices at the rebuke of a sincere wise man, and is not pleased with the song of fools, that is, their flattery of him with honeyed words, for it is like thorns under a pot, which give out sounds but burn and become ashes that we long to be rid of.

7.3.2.en: The wise man, who cares for the salvation of his soul, its edification and its constant growth, not only accepts the counsels of the wise but submits willingly to his discipline and his rebuke, for "reproofs of instruction are the way of life" (Prov 6:23); but the foolish man does not care about his eternity, so he is pleased with a life of pleasure and luxury and responds to the laughter of fools, a sign of the emptiness of his heart. The wise man says: "The end of that mirth is heaviness" (Prov 14:13). And the Lord Christ says: "Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh... Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep" (Lk 6:21, 25).

7.4.0.en: "Surely oppression maketh a wise man mad; and a gift destroyeth the heart" [7].

7.4.1.en: If we gladly accept the rebuke of a sincere wise man who cares for the salvation of our souls, then on our part we must not be harsh to others under the cover of "the rebuke of the wise," because much oppression can make a wise man mad, that is, drive him to deviation. Therefore the Psalmist says: "For the rod of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous; lest the righteous put forth their hands unto iniquity" (Ps 125:3).

7.4.2.en: As oppression may break the righteous, so the other extreme, "a gift destroyeth the heart" [7], perhaps here means giving lavishly without wisdom, or bribery, for it drives the soul to deviation.

7.4.3.en: * It is better to receive a rebuke from a wise man than to hear a whole chorus of the wretched in their songs, for the laughter of fools is like the crackling of many thorns burning in a blazing fire.

7.5.0.en: 8 Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. 9 Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools. 10 Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these? for thou dost not enquire wisely concerning this.

7.5.1.en: Among the counsels the Preacher offers to support man in preparing his soul for eternity are the following:

7.6.s.en: a. Not living on the dreams of the past:

7.6.0.en: "Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof" [8]. With the eye of faith we endure to the end and are saved. We do not stop at our striving in the past, nor despair at our weakness in the present, but we must work by the Spirit of God, confident that He will surely give us victory as long as we are in His hands, trusting in Him. The prophet Moses appeared to be a failure in his ministry even after God called him and sent him to Pharaoh... but in the end he achieved unexpected success. And St. Mark also left the ministry and returned to Jerusalem (Acts 13:13), but he came back and preached in many lands and bore much fruit... On the contrary, the Apostle Paul declares his sorrow for those who began in the Spirit and were made perfect in the flesh.

7.7.0.en: "The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit" [8]. It is as though patience of spirit, or longsuffering, is bound up with humility and is the opposite of the spirit of arrogance and pride or irritability, whether within the heart or outwardly. For by pride we lose our inner peace and our eternal inheritance.

7.7.1.en: * Patience (longsuffering) is the parent of consolation, and a special power that springs from constant breadth of heart; it is hard for a man to find that power in his afflictions unless it is given him by God. He receives this gift by his earnest, continual prayers and the shedding of tears.

7.7.2.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian * There is no healing for the pain of the proud, for the more he exalts himself in his thoughts, the more the knowledge of God departs from his soul, and he descends into the depth of darkness!

7.7.3.en: St. John Saba * Pride springs from the love of money, and from the conduct that arises from it...

7.7.4.en: What madness! Does this proud man not know that his glory passes away and evaporates like a dream, and that greatness and power are nothing but a deceptive mirage?!

7.8.0.en: "Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools" [9].

7.8.1.en: It behooves us to be cautious and not hasten to anger against others, because anger rests in the bosom of fools, meaning that it is born of ignorance and folly and finds its rest in it as an infant rests in its mother's bosom.

7.9.0.en: * The deadly poison of anger must be uprooted from the depths of our souls. For as long as it remains in our hearts and blinds with its harmful darkness the eye of the spirit (the heart), we cannot obtain discernment and sound judgment. Nor can we obtain true inward vision or perfect counsel, nor be partakers of life or keep righteousness, nor even have the capacity for true spiritual light, "Mine eyes are troubled by anger" (Ps 6:7). "Nor can we become partakers of wisdom, even if there should be a common verdict that we are wise, for anger resteth in the bosom of fools" [10], nor can we obtain the immortal life... "for anger destroys even judgment" (Prov 15:1). Nor can we obtain the restraining power of righteousness even if men think us perfect and holy, "for the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:20)... nor can we obtain even the honor and esteem that are in the world, even if they count us nobles and men of honor, "for the wrathful man is despised" (Prov 11:25)... nor can we be free from any disturbance even if no one has caused us disturbance... for "an angry man stirreth up strife, and a furious man aboundeth in transgression."

7.10.s.en: d. Not being swallowed up by the past at the expense of the present:

7.10.0.en: From the events of the past we learn God's rich grace through the ages, but we must not blame the present as though God had changed; rather we blame ourselves for our weaknesses, confident that the God who worked with us in the past is able to work also in the present.

7.10.1.en: "Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these?

7.10.2.en: for thou dost not enquire wisely concerning this" [10].

7.10.3.en: Let us thank God for His dealings with us in the past, and let us ask Him to work also in the present, feeling that our present existence is a divine gift, a blessing and an opportunity to receive better blessings.

7.10.4.en: The spiritual man feels that the moment he is living now is the most enjoyable moment of his life and the happiest in the Lord, realizing that it has been granted him for his repentance and spiritual growth, not that he may be occupied with the past and grieve over it as something lost, or as a happiness that has departed from him!

7.11.0.en: 11 Wisdom is good like an inheritance, yea better for them that see the sun. 12 For he that is in the shadow of wisdom is in the shadow of silver, and the excellency of knowledge is that wisdom giveth life to them that have it.

7.11.1.en: After presenting to us practical counsels to live by, that we may live happy in this passing life and as those being qualified for the other life... now he asks us to seek wisdom and acquire it, and perhaps he means by wisdom also the Second Hypostasis: the Word of God and His wisdom.

7.11.2.en: "Wisdom is good like an inheritance, yea better for them that see the sun" [11].

7.11.3.en: Some translate it: "Wisdom is good with an inheritance," so it is good not only for the poor, giving them contentment and thanksgiving so that they find rest, but also good for the rich, teaching them how to use their money and manage it and make with it friends who will receive them into everlasting habitations (Lk 16:9). By wisdom we profit from money and gain others by it as we gain our own souls.

7.11.4.en: By wisdom also we realize that God is our eternal inheritance, and we are His portion.

7.11.5.en: By wisdom we meet the Lord Christ, the Sun of righteousness, and the eyes of our hearts are enlightened, so that our bodies see the material sun and our hearts see the Sun of righteousness... our inner enlightenment is better than outer enlightenment!

7.12.0.en: "For he that is in the shadow of wisdom is in the shadow of silver, and the excellency of knowledge is that wisdom giveth life to them that have it" [12].

7.12.1.en: If man takes refuge in silver as a shadow that protects him from many troubles, and resorts to it to buy his food and drink and clothing and also his medicine... he truly needs wisdom as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land (Isa 32:2); it is like a wall and a hedge that protects the field of the soul from the raids of enemies. And what is greater, silver does not give life to those who have it, but may even kill them if they misuse it, while divine wisdom offers us life. Therefore "How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!" (Prov 16:16).

7.12.2.en: * For the excellence of man's life does not consist in acquiring passing wealth but in acquiring wisdom. It is the greatest of all the good things obtained from God, and when we dwell in it we do not sin.

7.12.3.en: * Wisdom helps more than a company of the strongest men of the city, and it often truly forgives those who fail in their duty.

7.12.4.en: St. Gregory the Wonder-worker * For as the Preacher says: "Wisdom is a defence (shadow) as money is a defence" [12]. It behooves us not to hasten to think that this saying contradicts the word of the Lord: "Verily I say unto you, That a rich man shall hardly enter into the kingdom of heaven. And again I say unto you, It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God" (Mt 19:23-24), because if it were so, the salvation of Zacchaeus the tax collector, described in the Holy Bible as a man of great wealth, would contradict the Lord's declaration!

7.13.0.en: 13 Consider the work of God: for who can make that straight, which he hath made crooked? 14 In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider: God also hath set the one over against the other, to the end that man should find nothing after him. 15 All things have I seen in the days of my vanity: there is a just man that perisheth in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man that prolongeth his life in his wickedness.

7.13.1.en: The writer summarizes his philosophy of life: since our life is in the hand of God, the Almighty, Father, wise and powerful, let us therefore thank Him in the days of joy, and seek His wisdom in the day of discipline... for in His love He gives us blessings, and we thank Him, and disciplines, and we profit by them; for our edification He allows this and that.

7.13.2.en: "I make peace, and create evil (affliction): I the LORD do all these things" (Isa 45:7).

7.13.3.en: "Consider the work of God: for who can make that straight, which he hath made crooked?!

7.13.4.en: In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider.

7.13.5.en: God also hath set the one over against the other, to the end that man should find nothing after him" [13-14].

7.13.6.en: The Preacher asks man to consider the work of God before he objects or murmurs. Neither money nor friends nor talents can change our nature and set right its crookedness and corruption, but God alone in His wisdom, as the Savior, knows how to tame us at one time by temporal blessings and at another by disciplines... and in both cases it is He who works in us. He sets this over against that, that is, He mixes days of ease with affliction, so that it is impossible for man to discover (find) what will happen to him tomorrow, and so he is always ready, trusting in God his Savior. In other words, it is to our good to accept the wisdom of God, which is able to set right our nature, without murmuring at the events that befall us.

7.13.7.en: Finally the Preacher offers his personal experience in this matter: in the days of his vanity, that is, the days in which he turned aside from God, he did not understand why the righteous are not delivered from afflictions while God is very patient with the wicked, so that it seems there is no justice or fairness.

7.13.8.en: "All things have I seen in the days of my vanity.

7.14.0.en: There is a just man that perisheth in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man that prolongeth his life in his wickedness" [15].

7.14.1.en: The righteous man may die at an early age, perhaps because God has seen him as a ripe fruit whose time for plucking has come, which would spoil if it remained on the tree. Many are taken by the Lord early to protect them from a coming evil, for the righteous is taken away from the face of evil. And God may allow the wicked to live and grow old and become mighty in strength, giving them the opportunity to repent or to fill up the cup of their wickedness.

7.15.0.en: 16 Be not righteous over much; neither make thyself over wise: why shouldest thou destroy thyself? 17 Be not over much wicked, neither be thou foolish: why shouldest thou die before thy time? 18 It is good that thou shouldest take hold of this; yea, also from this withdraw not thine hand: for he that feareth God shall come forth of them all. 19 Wisdom strengtheneth the wise more than ten mighty men which are in the city. 20 For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not. 21 Also take no heed unto all words that are spoken; lest thou hear thy servant curse thee: 22 For oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others.

7.15.1.en: When the Preacher calls us to wisdom, he is calling us to the moderate royal road, without extremism or deviation to the right or to the left, for the moderate way is the safe way that brings us into eternity.

7.15.2.en: "Be not righteous over much; neither make thyself over wise.

7.15.4.en: Be not over much wicked, neither be thou foolish.

7.15.5.en: Why shouldest thou die before thy time?" [16-17].

7.15.6.en: What does he mean by saying: "Be not righteous over much"? Be not excessive or extreme, but walk in righteousness with deliberation, wisdom and discernment. We mention by way of example:

7.15.7.en: a. Fasting is a godly spiritual exercise, but whoever abstains from foods as something defiled or unclean falls into heresy and error (1 Tim 4:3-4). And whoever exaggerates in his fasting and so loses his ability to work and to worship has misbehaved.

7.15.8.en: * We must place the purity of our souls in one pan of the scale and our bodily strength in the other, and weigh them by the judgment of our just conscience, so that we do not incline, deviating to one pan at the expense of the other, that is, to an unseemly strictness or an excessive relaxation.

7.15.9.en: Abba Theophas b. Reading the Holy Bible is necessary, but being absorbed in it for long periods on the nights of examinations is an escape from responsibility and not righteousness.

7.15.10.en: c. Virginity is a holy way for those who have this gift... but whoever walks this way and in extremism looks upon marriage as defiled or as something despised brings danger upon himself.

7.15.11.en: * Be not righteous over much, but rather give place to faith in your mind.

7.15.12.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian * The Apostle (Paul), at the end of his discussion of marriage and virginity, was careful to show a discernment between them without turning to the right or to the left, following the royal road, fulfilling the commandment: "Be not righteous over much."

7.15.13.en: St. Jerome Abba Theonas sees, in his Conferences with St. John Cassian, and so also St. Augustine, that the phrase "Be not righteous over much" refers to those who exaggerate the outward signs of religiosity and works of righteousness for the sake of the praise of men... such people appear as wise men while they are destroying themselves by the love of vainglory.

7.15.14.en: The enemy of good knows how to destroy souls: he ruins some by stinginess under the cover of wisdom, management and discipline, and others by squandering under the cover of generosity and simplicity, and some by exaggeration in fasting and the other kinds of worship out of a desire for vainglory; and some by constant preoccupation with service at the expense of their private relationship with God under the cover of witnessing to the Lord Christ, and others by isolating themselves in their rooms while closing their hearts to their brethren under the cover of personal worship... and so on... He knows how to urge man in one way or another to turn aside from the moderate, holy royal life in the Lord.

7.15.15.en: As for his counsel to the wicked, it is not to exploit the longsuffering of God, who sometimes allows the days of the wicked to be prolonged [15]. It does not befit them to continue in evil but to offer repentance, for in this is folly and the killing of the soul and the body also... "Neither be thou foolish: why shouldest thou die before thy time? [17].

7.16.0.en: He calls us to a life of wisdom and moderation without slackness in the life of virtue and striving, for by this we escape the two deviations: excessive righteousness and continuing in evil. For he says: "It is good that thou shouldest take hold of this; yea, also from this withdraw not thine hand: for he that feareth God shall come forth of them all" [18].

7.16.1.en: As the Preacher speaks of moderation he shows us the broad lines of this way:

7.17.0.en: a. The use of a spirit of wise meekness, not domination: for many who think themselves righteous and wise seek positions in the world or in the Church, hoping that through authority they may be able to set others right, therefore the wise man calls us not to seek authority but to walk in wise love, for "Wisdom strengtheneth the wise more than ten mighty men which are in the city" [19].

7.17.1.en: * God does not dwell in the lover of preeminence, nor do you dwell with him.

7.18.0.en: St. John Saba b. Confession of sin: The wise, moderate man does not look at himself as one without sin, judging and condemning others in a spirit of authority and rebuke, but feels their weakness because he shares the same weaknesses with them. No man, even a righteous one, is without sin as long as he is in the flesh and lives on earth. "For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not" [20]. The Apostle John says: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves" (1 Jn 1:8). So it behooves all, priests, teachers and people, to confess their need of God, the Savior of the world.

7.18.1.en: * The man who is aware of his sins is greater than he who profits the whole world, and this shows in his countenance. And he who sighs over himself for one hour is greater than he who raises the dead by his prayer while living among men.

7.18.2.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian * Who among men, even if we think him a chief of the righteous saints, can at some time, while bound with the chains of this life, reach this chief good without ceasing from holy contemplation?! Is he not drawn away, if only for a short time, from Him who alone is good by earthly thoughts...?!

7.18.3.en: Who among us, even in the moment when he lifts himself up in prayer to God and soars, never falls into distraction...?!

7.18.4.en: Therefore all the saints grieve with daily sighs over this weakness of their nature. And while they search their wandering thoughts and the hidden things of their consciences and their deep solitudes, they cry out in supplication: "Enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 143:2); "Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin?" (Ps 20:9)... "Who can understand his errors?!" (Ps 19:12). Thus they realized that man's righteousness is sickly and imperfect and always needs the mercy of God, so that one of them, after seeing the Seraphim on high and discovering the heavenly secrets, said: "Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips" (Isa 6:5)...

7.18.5.en: You see then how all the saints sincerely confess that all men, as they themselves, are sinners, and yet they never despair of their salvation, but seek complete cleansing by the grace and mercy of God.

7.18.6.en: * There is no one, however holy, in this life without sin. The teaching of the Savior, who gave His disciples the pattern of perfect prayer, has also told us so... when we say: "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" (Mt 6:12).

7.18.7.en: Abba Theonas c. Not being occupied with the words of others against you: He who walks in the righteousness of Christ does not care about the words of others, otherwise he would deviate into practicing righteousness to excess... for he who inclines his ear to the words of men finds that even those under his authority, even those to whom he provides their needs, curse him. In other words, let us be occupied with our eternity in our worship, in our teaching of others and in our daily conduct, and not care about the praise or blame of men, not because they are wicked, but because we ourselves in our weakness sin against others, even against those who do good to us.

7.19.0.en: "Also take no heed unto all words that are spoken; lest thou hear thy servant curse thee: for oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others" [21-22].

7.20.0.en: 23 All this have I proved by wisdom: I said, I will be wise; but it was far from me. 24 That which is far off, and exceeding deep, who can find it out? 25 I applied mine heart to know, and to search, and to seek out wisdom, and the reason of things, and to know the wickedness of folly, even of foolishness and madness: 26 And I find more bitter than death the woman, whose heart is snares and nets, and her hands as bands: whoso pleaseth God shall escape from her; but the sinner shall be taken by her. 27 Behold, this have I found, saith the preacher, counting one by one, to find out the account: 28 Which yet my soul seeketh, but I find not: one man among a thousand have I found; but a woman among all those have I not found. 29 Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions.
